input.raw_text: I traded through 2008 and I have never seen anything like this stretch. Circuit breakers have tripped at the open more than once this week, the S&P is down roughly thirty percent in a month, and the strangest part is what is being sold: ten-year yields have backed up toward 1.2% from record lows, gold has been dumped, and everyone is scrambling for dollar cash — funds, dealers, even sovereign accounts. The Fed cut to zero and launched massive asset purchases, swap lines with other central banks just got cheaper and longer, and Congress is still haggling, but the bid never shows up where it should. Treasury futures bid-ask is embarrassing, money is hiding in bills and repo, and liquidity, not solvency, is the immediate enemy.
input.summary: Extreme cross-asset stress combines a roughly thirty-percent monthly S&P decline and repeated opening circuit breakers with selling in Treasuries and gold, intense demand for dollar cash, impaired Treasury futures liquidity, and concentration in bills and repo. Large monetary interventions have not restored expected market demand, while the fiscal response remains unresolved and immediate pressure appears centered on liquidity rather than solvency.

interpretation.summary: The severe monthly equity decline and repeated circuit breakers weakly support bear and extreme-variance HMM behavior, while the sustained equity fall weakly supplies the activation condition for a trend-following state. Neither candidate has its model-specific performance or classification measurements in the packet. The remaining candidates require option data, cross-sectional liquidity statistics, serial-correlation estimates, corrected correlations, or financial-sector return panels that are not supplied.

citations.text: The measured SR/turnover tradeoff profile as the EWMM span parameter s varies across candidate values {15, 30, 60}. At s=15, EWMM features are highly responsive to recent returns, producing frequent HMM regime transitions and high daily portfolio turnover (ranging approximately 1.64% to 4.87% for some instruments), which erodes net SR under realistic transaction costs. At s=30, the tradeoff is favorable: daily turnover averages approximately 2.54% for comparable instruments and OOS SR exceeds 1 for most of the 15 futures instruments. At s=60, excessive feature smoothing slows regime detection, causing the strategy to lag genuine regime shifts and reducing OOS SR. The observable signature is the SR/turnover tradeoff curve itself: a characteristic shape with a favorable interior region (approximately s=25 to s=45) and degradation at both extremes. This tradeoff is measurable from any rolling OOS backtest by varying span across a grid while holding all other model parameters fixed. Applicable uniformly across the 15 multi-asset futures instruments at 5bps transaction costs (Nguyen 2021, Sections 4.2, 5). ewmm_span_parameter; daily_portfolio_turnover; oos_sharpe_ratio_by_span; net_sr_after_transaction_costs The favorable span range (approximately s=25-45) is identified on OOS testing over 2016-2019 with 5bps transaction costs. The optimal span is expected to be cost-environment and instrument dependent: higher transaction costs will favor larger spans to reduce turnover; lower-latency execution may shift the optimal span toward lower values. The tradeoff curve is the primary diagnostic for span calibration; it should be re-evaluated when deploying to new instruments or substantially different cost environments. Source is a preprint.

The Predicted Expected Sharpe Ratio (PESR) scalar signal and associated out-of-sample risk-adjusted return performance across multi-asset futures. PESR is defined as PESR = (ESR)^T * alpha_{n+h|n}, where ESR_j is the state-level expected Sharpe ratio estimated from EWMM features in hidden state j, and alpha_{n+h|n} = alpha_{n|n} * A^h is the h-step-ahead predicted state probability vector computed by multiplying the current filtered state vector by the h-th power of the transition matrix A. PESR is a scalar forward-looking risk-adjusted return predictor; positions are set proportional to its sign and magnitude (long-only: max(0, PESR)). OOS long-only strategy (Jan 2016 – Oct 2019, span=30, 5bps transaction costs) achieves substantially higher Sharpe ratios than buy-and-hold for most of 15 futures instruments: EQ4 SR=3.0 vs. B&H 1.0; FI1 SR=1.91 vs. 0.27; CO1 SR=2.4 vs. 0.67 (Nguyen 2021, Tables 3-4). pesr_scalar_signal; hmm_predicted_state_probability_h_step; state_level_expected_sharpe_ratio; oos_sharpe_ratio; buy_and_hold_sharpe_ratio PESR is both the decision rule (translating regime probabilities into positions) and the performance signal (higher OOS SR when PESR accurately predicts regimes). OOS test period is relatively short (approximately 4 years, Jan 2016–Oct 2019). Source is a preprint, not peer-reviewed. The combination of preprint source and short OOS window warrants some evidence discount, though the magnitude of SR improvement across multiple asset classes is striking.

matched_states.state_summary: A three-state hidden Markov model (HMM) regime structure applied asset- independently to daily futures returns across commodity, currency, equity, and fixed income classes. The three states are labeled bull (positive return, moderate volatility), bear (negative or flat return, elevated volatility), and high-volatility (extreme variance). The model uses EWMM (exponentially weighted moving moment) features of first and second return moments, normalized and concatenated independently per instrument, as the observation vector. Applied uniformly to 15 futures instruments (4 commodity, 4 currency, 4 equity, 3 fixed income) using 4972 daily observations (January 2000 – October 2019). Three states selected via greedy model selection. The PESR metric (Predicted Expected Sharpe Ratio) translates HMM-predicted state probabilities into a forward-looking scalar risk-adjusted return forecast by combining state-level SR estimates with h-step-ahead transition matrix powers. OOS long-only strategy (Jan 2016 – Oct 2019) achieves substantially higher Sharpe ratios than buy-and-hold across most instruments at 5bps transaction costs (e.g., EQ4: SR=3.0 vs. 1.0 B&H). EWMM span=30 provides a favorable SR/turnover tradeoff (Nguyen 2021 preprint).
matched_states.title: Three-State HMM Market Regime (Bull / Bear / High-Volatility)

citations.text: Observable monotone gradient of individual-asset Sharpe ratios with time-series momentum look-back horizon, combined with a large diversification benefit in a multi-asset portfolio. The signature is detectable as: (1) individual-asset TSMOM Sharpe ratios increasing from 0.29 (1-month horizon) to 0.36 (3-month) to 0.38 (12-month), averaged across 58 liquid futures contracts (commodities, equities, bonds, currencies), confirming that longer look-back windows capture more persistent trend signals; (2) the diversified portfolio Sharpe (~1.8 gross at 10% vol target) substantially exceeding the individual-asset average (0.38), demonstrating large cross-asset diversification benefit; (3) the portfolio achieves approximately 18% gross annualized return at 10% vol. Computed over January 1985–June 2012. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010). tsmom_1m_sharpe_individual; tsmom_3m_sharpe_individual; tsmom_12m_sharpe_individual; diversified_portfolio_sharpe; annualized_volatility_target; cross_asset_diversification_ratio The horizon-Sharpe gradient (0.29 / 0.36 / 0.38) is computed at the individual instrument level. The diversified portfolio at 12-month horizon achieves ~1.8 gross Sharpe, implying a diversification gain of approximately 4.7x relative to the individual-asset average (0.38). All figures are gross of fees and transaction costs; net returns are materially lower under 2-and-20 fee structures (see failure_hurst_mf_fee_erosion_003).

Observable pattern in managed futures fund TSMOM factor loadings revealing systematic underexposure to the individually optimal long-horizon (12-month) signal and overexposure to the suboptimal 3-month signal. The signature is detectable as: (1) regression of CTA fund net returns on the 1m, 3m, and 12m TSMOM factors shows the 3-month factor carrying the highest average loading across funds, despite the 12-month signal having the highest individual- asset Sharpe (0.38 vs. 0.36 and 0.29); (2) R-squared of 0.36–0.64 for individual fund returns on the diversified TSMOM factor, confirming that systematic trend following explains the majority of return variation while leaving unexplained residual variation potentially attributable to asset class tilts; (3) elevated fixed income factor loading relative to an equal- volatility multi-asset benchmark—indicating systematic overweight of bond futures relative to the theoretical optimum; (4) net-of-fee alpha becoming negative for all funds after TSMOM factor control, confirming that the loading pattern explains essentially all of net return. Estimated from CTA fund database regression analysis, approximately 1985–2012. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010). cta_fund_beta_to_tsmom_1m; cta_fund_beta_to_tsmom_3m; cta_fund_beta_to_tsmom_12m; cta_fund_r_squared_vs_tsmom; cta_fund_fixed_income_weight; cta_fund_net_alpha_post_tsmom The 3-month dominant loading across CTAs may reflect rational adaptation to operational constraints (AUM-driven capacity limits at shorter horizons force migration away from the shortest signals; client preference for lower volatility implementations may favor medium-length horizons). The fixed income overweight reflects the dominant bond bull market of 1985–2012 which benefited any fund with above-benchmark bond exposure. The loading pattern provides a diagnostic for identifying horizon-biased managed futures programs relative to the empirically optimal 12-month dominant allocation.

matched_states.state_summary: A market condition in which time-series momentum (TSMOM) signals deliver persistent risk-adjusted excess returns across diversified multi-asset futures portfolios. Characterized by: (1) individual-asset Sharpe ratios that increase monotonically with signal look-back horizon—0.29 (1-month), 0.36 (3-month), 0.38 (12-month)—averaged across 58 liquid futures contracts; (2) a diversified 58-instrument TSMOM portfolio achieving ~1.8 gross annualized Sharpe at 10% vol target (January 1985–June 2012); (3) a "smile" return pattern—best performance in sustained trending environments (strong bull or bear markets), worst in trendless choppy markets—with near-zero S&P 500 correlation (~-0.02); (4) after controlling for a simple diversified TSMOM factor, all managed futures fund net-of-fee alphas become negative under 2-and-20 fee structures (~6% average annual fee drag). Most CTAs exhibit dominant exposure to the 3-month TSMOM signal rather than the individually optimal 12-month horizon, and systematically overweight fixed income. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010), evidence_tier 2 (practitioner paper with direct empirical content).
matched_states.title: Multi-Asset Time-Series Momentum Trend Following State
